The statement recognizes a large negative real shock from COVID-19 and tightening global financial conditions—historically associated with deflationary risk—implying a weaker near-term outlook. However, the Fed’s rapid move to a 0–0.25% target range, sizable Treasury/MBS purchases, lower IOER and discount rates, expanded repos, and coordinated dollar swap lines is consistent with research that countercyclical monetary policy can dampen fluctuations and support the real economy when shocks hit. The credit-view literature (e.g., work highlighted by Oliner and Rudebusch; evidence on small-firm financing by Gertler and Gilchrist; and inventory-investment sensitivity by Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein) emphasizes that easing funding strains lowers the external finance premium and stabilizes business investment and household spending. 

While market-based inflation compensation fell, survey-based long-term expectations are little changed, aligning with the idea that a credible central bank and inflation-targeting/forecast-targeting frameworks keep expectations anchored (Svensson) and mitigate inflationary bias under discretion (Rogoff). Given liquidity-trap risks, deploying the balance sheet and forward-looking commitments is also consistent with the literature’s guidance. 

Net assessment: the near-term outlook is still negative, but the policy response meaningfully offsets downside risks relative to an unmitigated scenario.
